title: Is the Shannon capacity of a graph computable?
premise_risks: Phrasing as 'decide' - both answers would be major; scorer may see it as famous/very hard
plain: The Shannon capacity Theta(G) of a finite graph is the limit of alpha(G^k)^{1/k}, where alpha is the independence number of the k-th strong power. Every alpha(G^k) is computable, so one can list ever better lower bounds, but no algorithm is known that produces upper bounds converging to Theta(G). Decide whether some algorithm, given G and a rational q, halts exactly when Theta(G) < q (equivalently, whether Theta is a computable function).
math: Encode finite simple graphs and rationals as natural numbers and let $\Theta(G)=\sup_k\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}$. Determine whether $U=\{(G,q):\Theta(G)<q\}$ is recursively enumerable. (Since $\{(G,q):\Theta(G)>q\}$ is r.e., $U$ is r.e. iff $G\mapsto\Theta(G)$ is a computable real-valued function.) A weaker open subquestion: is $\Theta(G)$ a computable real for every $G$ (e.g. $G=C_7$)?
